newsitem.title: ITALY: Generali and Alleanza get share boost from results.
newsitem.headline: Generali and Alleanza get share boost from results.

text.p: Shares in two of Italy's largest insurers Generali and Alleanza rose sharply on Tuesday as their results appeared to signal a revival in the fortunes of the two linked groups into 1997, analysts said.

Results late Monday showed an underlying 14.3 percent rise in 1996 net profits at Italy's largest insurer Generali, while Alleanza, 64 percent Generali-owned, saw 1996 net profits up 60 percent while first quarter 1997 premiums rose 35.3 percent.

Analysts said that the underlying rise in Generali's profits came as a welcome surprise to the Milan stock market, while investors warmed to the progress that Alleanza had made in Italy's largely underdeveloped life insurance market.
Generali shares were quoted 2.5 percent firmer at 30,500 lire at 1400 GMT, while Alleanza shares were 4.07 percent higher at 12,265 lire in an overall slightly firmer Milan bourse.

Generali said late Monday its net consolidated attributable profit rose to 1.437 trillion lire ($856 million) from 695 billion lire in 1995, and even without the proceeds from its sale of a stake in French insurer AXA its underlying profits would have been up 14.3 percent at 800 billion lire.

The insurer based in Trieste in northeast Italy which is Europe's third largest insurer after French AXA UAP and German Allianz, said 1996 premiums rose 10.7 percent to 34.924 trillion lire, with 30.1 percent from Italy.

The nation's biggest life insurance company Alleanza, with a 11.7 percent market share, on the same day said its 1996 net consolidated 1996 income rose 60 percent to 246.7 billion lire from 1995's figure of 154.2 billion lire.
Premium and related income rose 12 percent in 1996 from 1995 and in the first three months of 1997 premium income rose even faster to show the 35.3 percent increase.
Insurance industry analysts focused on the underlying rise in Generali's 1996 profits of over 14 percent, and the first quarter accelerated growth in premiums at Alleanza.
"These were positive results, there was a decrease in Generali's expenses ratio while the loss ratio was stable," said analyst Paola Buratti at brokers Indosuez.
Analysts said that the Italian market is a relatively underdeveloped market for insurance products, especially life insurance, with plenty of potential for growth.

One industry analyst in London said the weakness in both stocks over the past year had more to do with concerns over asset values in the companies rather than with the potential of the Italian insurance market. However, all was not positive among Italian insurance stocks with the shares of Italy's largest motor insurer SAI falling after it reported on late Monday. The shares were donw 2.63 percent at 11,980 lire.

SAI said its 1996 net profit rose to 94.1 billion lire against 92.1 billion lire in 1995, on premium income which increased 20 percent to 4.607 trillion lire, and proposed a unchanged ordinary share dividend of 200 lire a share. ($1=1,679 lire)
